source_document.body:
DoorDash’s move into retail returns raises a practical question: Will shoppers pay $7.99 to skip a trip to drop off a package? In this Q&A, Andrew Schmid , Chief Product Officer at Route and a former Nike retail executive, discusses what makes doorstep returns worth the price, what retailers need to handle behind the scenes, and how to measure whether the service is working.
What’s Related
Supply Chain 24/7: What stands out to you about DoorDash’s new retail returns service?
Andrew Schmid: What stands out to me is that DoorDash is moving further into a part of retail that has historically been pretty fragmented. Returns are a huge expense for retailers, and getting a product from someone's doorstep back into the supply chain is only one piece of that. I think we'll see more delivery and logistics companies trying to own more of the customer experience, especially as competition heats up. The new question, though, is whether that added convenience creates enough value for shoppers and retailers to justify yet another cost in the returns process.
SC247: Will shoppers pay $7.99 for a return pickup?
Schmid: I think some shoppers absolutely will, but it depends on what they're returning and how much hassle the service saves them. If I'm returning a $200 pair of shoes and don't have time to get to a drop-off location, $7.99 might feel pretty reasonable. But for a $25 item, that's a much harder sell, especially when every dollar counts for consumers right now. Retailers also have to decide whether shoppers should pay for it, the brand should fund it or it should be a benefit for their most loyal customers.
SC247: What needs to happen behind the scenes between the pickup and the customer getting a refund?
Schmid: There's a lot more happening behind the scenes than most shoppers realize. The retailer needs to know the item was picked up, track it through the return process, determine when to issue a refund and decide what happens to that inventory once it comes back. When a refund is late, the shopper isn’t weighing whether the warehouse scan failed or the returns platform never got the update. They just want their money back. That requires the systems handling pickups, returns and refunds to all communicate with each other.
Andrew Schmid
SC247: What should retailers have in place before offering a service like this?
Schmid: I'd start by looking at how well your existing returns process works before adding another pickup option. A common challenge is that tracking, customer support, returns and exchanges often live in separate systems that aren’t connected. Adding DoorDash to that process creates another handoff, so retailers need to make sure pickup confirmations, return statuses and refund information actually get where they need to go. I'd want a clear understanding of which customers would use the service and whether the retailer can support the additional volume without creating more problems for its operations team. There’s also an unanswered question about cost: Does the shopper or the brand eat it?
SC247: Where do you see the highest costs, and what would it take to make this profitable?
Schmid: Having spent years working in retail operations, I can tell you the return label is only a fraction of the expense. You've got transportation , receiving, inspecting the product and then deciding whether it goes back into inventory, gets discounted or can't be resold at all. Each step adds another cost. Adding doorstep pickup creates another cost before the product even enters that process, so the economics have to make sense. I'd be looking at whether DoorDash can keep pickup costs down by combining returns with existing delivery routes and whether the service actually reduces costs elsewhere in the process. If it just makes an already expensive return more expensive, retailers will find it hard to sustain.
SC247: How could faster return pickups help retailers get products back on shelves and ready to sell again?
Schmid: Speed matters, especially for seasonal products or inventory that's only valuable for a short window. But getting an item off someone's doorstep faster doesn't necessarily mean it's available to sell again any sooner. It still needs to move through receiving, inspection and whatever process the retailer uses to get it back into inventory. A return physically received but never recorded is exactly the kind of operational gap that can erase the benefit of a faster pickup. Retailers need to look at how long the entire process takes, from the moment a shopper requests a return to when that product is actually available for someone else to buy.
SC247: How does adding returns change DoorDash’s competition with Uber and other delivery services?
Schmid: I think we're heading into a pretty interesting period of competition and consolidation across logistics. DoorDash and Uber have already built networks designed to move things quickly, and returns give them another opportunity to put that infrastructure to work. We're seeing a similar push toward consolidation with C.H. Robinson 's acquisition of RXO, as companies look for ways to offer more supply chain services. My question is how much of that expansion retailers actually need and whether the economics work. Amazon has the scale and logistics infrastructure to absorb rising fulfillment and delivery costs, but most retailers don't have that luxury.
SC247: For an e-commerce brand considering doorstep returns, what should it measure to decide whether the service is working?
Schmid: I'd want to understand how many shoppers are actually choosing doorstep pickup and what it's costing the retailer for each completed return. Then I'd look at whether products are getting back into sellable inventory faster, whether refund timelines are improving and whether customer service teams are seeing fewer questions about returns. Return and exchange rates, customer support inquiries, refund timelines and repeat purchase behavior give a much more complete picture of how the experience is working. Ultimately, retailers need to understand whether the convenience is valuable enough to customers to justify the cost, and whether it's helping them grow their business .
Andrew Schmid is Chief Product Officer at Route .
